Frames

Schema definition and guidance.

11%

Welfare and Safety

Animal Welfare and Injuries

Coverage centered on the physical risks to horses in the Grand National and measures to mitigate them (injuries, fatalities, welfare reforms, veterinary protocols, fence design, field size). Near-misses: spectator/weather safety; race operational inspections due to storms; betting-market ‘liability’ risk; celebrity commentary not about welfare. Decision rules — MUST: explicitly reference horse welfare, injury, death, risk, or safety measures for horses. SHOULD: mention the Grand National/Aintree fences or welfare groups/official reforms. SHOULD: include veterinary, fence, or field-size details. NEVER: pieces limited to weather-related event safety or postponements. NEVER: pieces primarily about betting odds/markets or fashion/celebrity without horse-risk context.

Keywords: animal welfare, horse welfare, safety of horses, equine safety, injury, injuries, fallers, fatality, fatalities, horse deaths, euthanised, put down, Becher’s Brook, Canal Turn, Aintree fences, fence modifications, vet checks, veterinary, equine ambulance, screens, whip rules, welfare groups, RSPCA, World Horse Welfare, dangerous, risk, field size, start procedures

Examples: Two horses were put down after falls at Becher’s Brook, reigniting welfare concerns.; Animal charities called for smaller fields and lower fences to improve horse safety.

41%

Betting and Odds

Betting and Odds

Coverage about gambling on the Grand National: odds, favorites, tips with prices, bookmaker offers, market moves, staking, and payouts. Near-misses: pure race previews without odds or betting language; attendance/celebrity/fashion pieces; safety/welfare reporting. Decision rules — MUST: include explicit betting/odds/bookmaker terms or price formats. SHOULD: name a bookmaker or include fractional/decimal odds or a stake/offer. SHOULD: include tips framed as bets (each-way/NAP) or market commentary. NEVER: if only social/fashion without gambling content. NEVER: if focused on horse welfare/safety without betting outcomes.

Keywords: bet, bets, betting, odds, price, prices, priced at, favourite, favorite, outsider, market, market mover, punter, punters, bookie, bookies, bookmaker, William Hill, Ladbrokes, BoyleSports, Betfair, Coral, Paddy Power, SP, starting price, ante-post, each-way, EW, accumulator, acca, NAP, tip, tips, free bet, price boost, cash-out, stake, wager, liability, payout

Examples: Free £2 William Hill shop bets on The Grand National in your local paper; Bookies are expecting a bumper year for AP McCoy’s last ever Grand National. Experts are predicting £200m worth of bets to be placed across the whole three days; a whopping £150m of that total coming from today’s Grand National race.

16%

Celebs and Style

Celebrities and Style

Coverage emphasizing celebrity attendance, fashion, photo-led social scene, and entertainment at the Grand National (e.g., Ladies Day, best-dressed, performers, hospitality). Near-misses: betting odds/tips; race analysis/results; welfare/safety debates. Decision rules — MUST: reference celebrities/attendees, fashion/style, social photos, or entertainment programming. SHOULD: mention "Ladies Day"/"best dressed"/performers/guest lists/venue hospitality. SHOULD: foreground attendees over sporting action. NEVER: if the piece is chiefly betting/odds or horse welfare/injury. NEVER: pure technical race previews/results without social angle.

Keywords: Ladies Day, fashion, style, best dressed, glamour, hats, fascinators, dress code, racegoers, crowd photos, spot yourself, photo gallery, celebrity, celeb, VIP, red carpet, guest list, hospitality, party, music act, performers, entertainment, Aintree style, social scene

Examples: Ladies Day at the Aintree Grand National Festival 2015.; In Pictures: Spot yourself at Ladies Day?

🔗📁‌ Racing returned to the home of the Randox Health Grand National for the first time in 321 days and outsider Real Stone landed the opening contest of the afternoon. ‌ Following the disappointment of the cancellation of the three-day Grand National Festival in April due to the coronavirus pandemic, it was good to see action at the famous Liverpool track, even if the sport continues to go on behind-closed doors. ‌ Skelton's five-year-old came through, under the trainer's brother Harry, to score by two and a half lengths from Colin Tizzard's Killer Stone (7-2) at Aintree. The Nigel Twiston-Davies-trained 7-4 favourite Torn And Frayed - owned by Southport-born Carl Hinchy - cut out the running the 2m4f contest with his chief market rivals Danny Kirwin (9-4) and Killer Kane just sitting off the pace. Real Stone was settled further back by Skelton.

🔗📁On the final turn for home Minellacelebration came through with former Grade Two Aintree winner Don Poli. ‌ Don Poli - formerly trained by Gordon Elliott and one of several horses in the field to have run in the Grand National in the past - went to the front. But the winner was always travelling the better. Poste brought him through to lead over the second last fence and he moved clear of his rivals. He came home to score by a comfortable 14 lengths from the Evan Williams-trained Pobbles Bay (14-1) with Paul Nicholls' Sametegal - sent off the 7-2 favourite - a neck back in third, the same place he occupied over the Grand National fences in the Grand Sefton Chase three years ago.

Changes to the course were introduced in 2012 and there were no fatalities between 2013 and 2018, but that has now increased to five in the last three runnings of the festival (2020 was cancelled due to Covid-19).

🔗📁“We’re doing all we can, honest guv.” That’s the industry’s response when confronted about the cruelty that’s inherent in their profiteering. Organisers and their lackeys repeat the same basic line – “everything that can be done is done” – but it’s simply not true. Race authorities have refused to implement the basic welfare measures that the League Against Cruel Sports has been requesting for the last five years. The rejected measures include reducing the number of riders from 40 to a maximum of 30; banning the use of whips; and removing all drops on the landing side of the fences.

🔗📁Crucially, the League has also asked for the removal of Aintree’s infamous Becher’s Brook jump, which is the deadliest obstacle on the course and generally considered the most dangerous jump in the world. The racecourse and British Horseracing Authority have refused to budge on this point. After all, the danger is what draws some people to watch. The industry did implement minor safety measures for the 2012 Grand National, including stricter pre-race screenings and tweaks to three of the fences. But two horses still died that year – Synchronised and According To Pete – and welfare groups have dismissed the changes as token gestures used to pull the wool over the eyes of the public.

🔗📁Racing folk love to tell us that they treat horses better than they treat humans. Well, in that case don’t let them anywhere near your loved ones. You can replace a horse.” It was as if a metaphorical tarpaulin, like the one race organisers scramble to drape over any horse that dies at the National, had been pulled away, revealing the ugly reality.

🔗📁But Walsh’s attitude reflects the commercial reality behind the scenes. Have you ever wondered what happens to the horses when they are no longer sprightly enough to race? A select few enjoy their retirement but an investigation by The Observer found the answer is often “a bullet through the temple or a metal bolt into the side of the brain” before the corpses are driven to France and sold as meat. Few who watch the National and other big-day races are aware of the suffering involved. Indeed, pointing it out can make you seem a killjoy. Well, better a killjoy than a horse killer, I say.

🔗📁Brian Volks from Dark Horse The Welsh ingenues may get subjected to turned-up noses by racing’s door-keeping functionaries. However, the owners and trainers themselves show them no prejudice. “There’s no snobbery at all with other racehorse owners because it’s such a precarious sport,” Howard Davies, the group’s treasurer, told the Guardian. “Everyone unites in that supportive mode.” So which analysis is the more telling? The left-leaning or the right? It’s when the chips are down that true colours are revealed. Following a run of successes, Dream, now insured at £180,000, is entered for a hurdle race at Aintree. Halfway through, he suddenly staggers. A hoof has sliced a tendon in his front leg. It seems certain he will never run again. A normal syndicate would have had him shot. Dream’s owners, however, decide otherwise.

🔗📁They’re told that stem-cell surgery might help Dream’s leg recover, though not enough to let him to return to racing. It would cost them £20,000, which they’d have no prospect of recovering. Unanimously, they decide to go ahead. Why? Johnson White from Dark Horse In the film, Jan explains that she considered Dream’s winnings to belong to him, not to his owners. For her, it’s the worker, not the investor, who has first call on the proceeds of his labour. Davies sees it slightly differently. For him, Dream was not so much an employee as a de facto syndicate member, earning equity through toil as in an employee share scheme. Either way, when it came to the crunch individual need trumped personal gain.

Aintree Racecourse will once again host the iconic steeplechase, which will be run for the 176th time. 🔗📁Any lingering doubt that Nicky Henderson would retain the National Hunt trainers’ championship appeared to be extinguished here on Thursday, as a Grade One treble took his prize money haul for the season past £3m and opened a gap to Paul Nicholls, the 10-times champion, that even a Grand National victory would fail to bridge. Henderson’s three winners in consecutive races included an easy success for Might Bite, the Cheltenham Gold Cup runner-up, in the Betway Bowl and a three-length victory in the Aintree Hurdle for L’Ami Serge, a horse whose appetite for a battle has sometimes been called into question. We Have A Dream, a 2-1 chance, set the ball rolling in the Anniversary Juvenile Hurdle.

🔗📁The ease of Might Bite’s success, which was sealed with a flourish as he flew the last fence, was all the more impressive in view of his hard race behind Native River on heavy ground at Cheltenham last month. He will now head to summer quarters as the ante‑post favourite for both the King George VI Chase and Gold Cup next season, while Henderson may also consider a run in the Betfair Chase in November to set up a possible tilt at a £1m bonus on offer for victory in all three races. “He’s been fresh and well since Cheltenham and you’d have thought he’d have been the one who wouldn’t be as he had such a gruelling race at the Festival,” Henderson said. “He’s not a fragile horse in any sense but you always have to be wary of his head, so it was quite brave coming here and I had my doubts. His jumping was an exhibition round. The plan will be the same next year and I’d love to have another crack at the Gold Cup on good ground.”

🔗📁This dramatic late development is bad luck on Sandown, used to attracting the very best for this Grade One two-mile showpiece; the last three winners of the race have gone on to land the Champion Chase at the Cheltenham Festival. This injury, to his off fore, is a new one, but Nicky Henderson was quick to rule him out of today’s contest. “It’s not going to mend overnight,” said the trainer before lamenting: “His work last Saturday was brilliant. Both Protektorat and Le Milos provided first successes in those prestigious contests and Ashtown Lad gave Skelton a first success over the big Aintree obstacles. ‌ Despite reservations over his stamina – he had faded to be fifth in the Coral Scottish Grand National at Ayr in April – Ashtown Lad, who is owned by Aintree lover Darren Yates, is likely to be aimed at the world’s greatest steeplechase back in Liverpool on April 15 in the New Year. He could be real contender for the big one if he stays the extra distance having taken to the unique challenge so well. He was cut to 33-1 by Paddy Power for the National behind last year's winner Noble Yeats, who is as low as 8-1 following his earlier impressive victory in the Many Clouds Chase on his return to Aintree.

🔗📁Harry Skelton always had Ashtown Lad well placed close up out wide as first Dr Kananga, then Cloth Cap led the field over the big Aintree obstacles. As Dr Kananga faded Ashtown Lad moved ahead of Cloth Cap and made his move for home. But the Oliver Greenall and Josh Guerriero-trained Gesskille – who had also been second over the fences in last month's Grand Sefton Chase – tried to bridge the gap. Although the latter was closing in all the time Ashtown Lad galloped all the way to the line to score by two-and-a-quarter-lengths from the 4-1 favourite. Percussion (10-1) was three-and-a-half lengths back in third with Fortescue (33-1) a further four-and-a-quarter lengths adrift in fourth with Five Star Getaway fifth and Cloth Cap in sixth.

🔗📁As day two of the Grand National gets underway, thousands of ladies dressed in outrageous or elegant outfits as they compete in the style stakes and take in some high-class racing throughout the day. Seven races make up the day as they saw Saphir Du Rheu, ridden by Sam Twiston-Davis, take home the Betfred Mildmay Novices' Chase and following up from his second place at the World Hurdle at Cheltenham festival. A.P McCoy rides Don Cossack and Eastlake in what is his last ever Grand National festival, as he looks to leave the racing scene and his legacy with a bang.

🔗📁Such episodes are something Aintree bosses had hoped to avoid this year, with the strict style code just one of a raft of measures designed to add some class to the image of the event which has suffered in recent years. Along with expecting 'Chanel-inspired' get-ups from female racegoers, the management has also threatened to kick out any photographers caught taking photos of drunken racegoers. 'Our event is full of character, it’s fun, and that’s generated by the personality of the Liverpool people,' said Aintree managing director John Baker in the run-up to this year's event. 'We have to absolutely protect that because it’s at the core of what we are, and we have a responsibility to our customers to project the correct image.'

🔗📁Dr Richard Newland is hopeful Pineau De Re is in the good enough form as he heads back to Aintree to defend his Crabbie’s Grand National crown. The 12-year-old is still on course for the world’s greatest steeplechase after he was among the remaining 74 entries left in the race after yesterday’s latest forfeit stage. Pineau De Re is a 25-1 chance with several firms including Ladbrokes, William Hill, BetVictor and Paddy Power to become the first horse since Red Rum in 1973-74 to win back-to-back renewals of the Grand National at Aintree two weeks on Saturday. Newland and Pineau De Re’s owner, Glaswegian John Provan, were both back at Aintree for the Northern Media Lunch when the latest entries were unveiled yesterday. And they are hopeful of enjoying more success.

🔗📁He finished 11th in the Pertemps Final at the Cheltenham Festival in his prep race earlier this month. He finished third in the same race prior to his National victory, but Newland was happy with that effort. He said: “His form is okay. It has been a different campaign to last year because last year we had to get into the race and we were racing a lot more. We had to win a race to qualify – which we did at Exeter. But this year we knew we would be in the race, so it was all about getting back in one piece. So we have deliberately gone slowly, slowly. Possibly too slowly, but I have been happy with his two runs. Two good runs over hurdles. Not many 12-year-old National winners could be running in Pertemps Finals and giving weight to horses who he is twice the age of. I think he has run well enough.”

🔗📁A penny for Harry Redknapp’s thoughts. The lamentable display from Ballyburn in the Browns Advisory Chase enabled Lecky Watson to grind out a shock victory on Wednesday and it will not have done anything to rid Redknapp of the sense of what have been. The Jukebox Man was going to be Ballyburn’s biggest challenger, following his fluent and precise victory in the Kauto Star Novices Chase on Boxing Day but a gallops injury led to him having surgery and ruling him out of the rest of the season. Trainer Ben Pauling recently told Mail Sport that The Jukebox Man’s rehabilitation is going smoothly and he is adamant the gelding will win big prizes next winter. If he had been fit, though, he could – and probably would – have landed a huge pot this week. It’s the one that got away.

🔗📁Monday’s best bets, by John O’Hara It’s Monday so it has to be Windsor, except it will be run in the afternoon and not the evening, which the racecourse is famous for – those long balmy summer evenings now consigned to the memory banks. Nevertheless there are some good betting opportunities, notably Vermuelen (3.50) in the extended 1m3f maiden. John Gosden’s charge didn’t show a great deal in his two runs last year, but looked a totally different prospect at Chelmsford on his return to action last month when only beaten half a length into second behind Beauty Sleep. The obvious danger is Plenary, trained by Jeremy Noseda. He is enduring a season similar to his handler in that he seems to have seconditis, having finished runner-up three times from four outings this season, and his trainer has had more seconds than winners. This looks like another race where they will find one better.

🔗📁Tipping competition – a new week Congratulations to goodfellow1, who held on to win last week’s competition on a final score of +11.38, despite a winnerless Friday. We’ll be in touch by email. Alas, we’re not going to be able to continue with these competitions every week and the one that starts today will be the last until the new year. A reorganisation of duties has meant we no longer have the time needed to keep scores while also obtaining and distributing prizes. We will still have competitions in the biggest weeks (Cheltenham, Aintree, Royal Ascot, Glorious Goodwood and maybe one or two others, as well as the Christmas quiz). And we’ll still have a Talking Horses each day for tips, analysis and news, so we very much hope you’ll join us to chew over whatever racing happens to be going on, especially those of you who have been in the habit of sharing winning tips at good prices.

🔗📁It’s been almost eight years since DrKelso won our very first competition, which is not a bad length of time to sustain something like this. Congratulations to all our winners since then, commiserations if you never quite got your nose in front; there will be fewer chances to break your duck now but there will still be chances, so stay with us. The prize for our final competition of 2016 is a copy of the new volume of Chasers & Hurdlers, to be published next month by Timeform. Running to 1,100 pages and retailing at £75, it is a big, beautiful record of the last jumps season, including many of the famous Timeform essays discussing the major performers and the issues raised during the winter. Evidently one of the essays suggests that some stewards are “blind … to non-triers”! If you don’t win, you can buy a copy here.

🔗📁The second bet you place is normally at a quarter of the odds but can sometimes be a fifth of the odds, particularly when bookmakers are paying out on a higher number of places. ‌ When placing a £1 each-way bet, you will have noticed that, in total, you parted with £2. With each-way betting, if your horse wins at 12/1 then you get £12 plus your £1 stake back. In addition to that, if your bookie is paying out at a quarter of the odds for a place, the £12 is divided by four - £3. So you get another £3 plus your £1 stake.

🔗📁Died: May 9 2019 FREDDIE Starr, who has died aged 76, was a comedian, impressionist and singer whose act was as volatile as his frequently erratic off-stage life. Starr had considerable natural gifts as a performer – he could be, and for many years was, a successful “straight” singer, a highly accomplished mimic and, many thought, one of the most impressive physical comics ever – but it was, above all, an air of danger and unpredictability which distinguished his performances. On chat shows, he was liable to impersonate and insult his fellow guests (which, bravely, once included Mohammed Ali, whom he reduced to tears of laughter), to remove his shoe and use it as a water glass (with Terry Wogan), or to wrestle the host into a fountain that formed the centrepiece of the set (with Des O’Connor). Faced with a theatre packed with celebrities for An Audience with Freddie Starr in 1996, he opened the proceedings by flinging handfuls of live maggots at them; this did not prevent him returning for Another Audience with Freddie Starr the following year.

🔗📁Starr then went solo, but was a surprise booking for the Royal Variety Performance of 1970, where he stole the show, drawing a standing ovation. Through the 1970s, though he continued to release records (he notched up several gold discs), he was increasingly viewed as a comic. His anarchic stage shows proved tricky to present on television, though persistent attempts were made, notably on Who Do You Do? (1972) and as a panellist on Jokers Wild. A planned series in 1974, however, was reduced to a single special, while Freddie Starr’s Variety Madhouse (1979) on which Russ Abbott was a sidekick, soon morphed into Russ Abbott’s Madhouse. Starr's fortunes were not helped by his struggle to overcome his longstanding addiction to painkillers, something he seemed to have managed by the mid-1980s.

🔗📁He was, however, a constant presence on chat shows and the live stage, and in the 1980s was one of the highest-earning performers in the country. In the early 1990s, he finally got his own shows, Freddie Starr (1993-4) and The Freddie Starr Show (1996-8), but much of his act – or the attitudes contained in it – already seemed dated, while the energy of his live appearances did not always translate to the small screen. From around the turn of the century, he was more often on game shows or reality programmes, such as Beat the Crusher (1999), Living with the Dead (2009) and Celebrity Fit Club (2004). Starr, sacked as team leader on the last, turned out not only to be unfit, but seriously unwell; in 2010 he had a heart attack and quadruple bypass surgery. The following year he was hospitalised while filming I’m a Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here in the Australian jungle, and left early.

Then, in 1998, Starr was arrested for punching his estranged son during a meeting to patch things up. The Yewtree allegations cast a shadow over his last years. Visibly aged, he moved permanently to the Costa del Sol, where he was found dead at home on May 9.
